newsitem.title: CANADA: FEATURE - Toronto oxygen bar plans to spread to New York, L.A..
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Toronto oxygen bar plans to spread to New York, L.A..

text.p: Lissa Charron wants to bring a breath of fresh air to smog-choked residents of New York and Los Angeles. The catch is she charges for it.

O2 Spa Bar, opened by Charron and partner Shamila Hunter in Toronto seven months ago, will open its first spin-off location in New York around Christmas. The tired, hungover and stressed-out who flop into the clean, open-plan bar can partake of freshly squeezed organic juices, listen to soothing jazz music, watch gently swimming tropical fish in a high-tech tank and grab a snootful of oxygen.

The bar with a difference offers a 20-minute dose of 99.9 percent pure oxygen in one of several fruit flavors at its curved marble bar. The same treatment, delivered through a sterile nose tube identical to that used by hospitals, can also be received in private spa rooms, each of which is painted a different color and sports a different fishtank.
The bar's massage therapists can also provide an oxygen facial or massage. Prices range from about $12 to just under $50, plus tax.

"We're so used to going into bars and doing things that aren't that good for us. It's part of our social setting," Charron, an interior designer and former competitive swimmer and model, told Reuters. "We're offering a smoky bar alternative where you can come in, either with a date or a friend ... into a really nice atmosphere and do something really good for yourself for a change."

Charron, 31, said her early clientele were mostly mobile Baby Boomers -- doctors, lawyers, supermodels, athletes and stockbrokers. But the bar attracted so much ink and celluloid -- particularly from U.S. popular media like People magazine and the Hard Copy tabloid television show -- in recent weeks that she now has a whole cross-section of customers.
The bar is visited by dancers and workout fiends as well as those suffering the effects of bad air, the overworked, overtired and hungover.

"We have some crazy Bay Street boys (financial district workers) that I guess have the seven-martini meetings in the evening and they come in here in the morning looking like death warmed over and it's like 'save me,'" Charron said.
A number of her visitors are American tourists who include the spa bar in their visit to Canada's largest city.

Media interest has had an important fringe benefit for the expansion-minded Charron. In one week, her chief financial officer received more than 200 franchising inquiries, she said. Hunter and Charron plan to open their next locations in New York, Los Angeles and Vancouver, British Columbia. Some they plan to own themselves, others they hope to franchise.
"New York and Los Angeles can definitely accomodate more than two or three O2 spa bars. We want to have a few in those cities ourselves and franchise the others," Charron said.

Many of the requests for franchise information have come from doctors, although Charron said she and her partner make no claim to be running a medical center. They recommend that those who call asking for a miracle cure for a specific illness go to their own doctors and request specialized help.

Bars that profess to supply oxygen are already popular in Beijing and Tokyo but Charron said there is a difference in what she is offering. "As far as we know, all the ones that we have researched are 'air bars,'" she said. "They call themselves oxygen bars but what they are giving the public is 21 percent oxygen, which is what we are breathing right now. We're the first people to give 99.9 percent pure oxygen, the good stuff."
The system they use to deliver the oxygen is a secret. Charron said it involved the efforts of eight medical installers, several engineers, a respirologist and registered respiratory therapists.
